connector: It’s Anne. I’m to go to Queen’s in three weeks, and Marilla has brought me the loveliest pale green stuff for an evening dress, which I don’t need at all, and Matthew keeps buying more. I used to say I was in the depths of despair about everything. Now I’m only very excited and a tiny bit frightened, which is much more sensible for a girl of sixteen.

guide2.label: Anne · before you open the book

transcripts.welcome: Hello, it’s Anne, and today’s question is about me, which feels very strange to say out loud. Who am I really, when everything is changing? I’ll try not to make a speech of it. First there’s word work, and you’ll be hunting for mistakes. Then you read about the day I leave Green Gables. Then you decide what stays the same. I’m still deciding myself.
transcripts.dol: The top sentence is about me, and I wish it weren’t quite so true. Lonesomer. Isn’t that a lovely, sad word? Find the joining verb, and the word that compares. The bottom sentence needs a stop in the middle and two capitals, one of them mine. I’d be grateful if you gave it back. A girl’s name ought to stand up straight, even when she’s homesick.
transcripts.guide1: This is the last day of word work this week, and nearly everything asks you to catch a mistake. Here’s a secret I learned at the Entrance: some of the sentences are perfectly right, and tapping those costs you. So don’t tap because you’re nervous. Tap because you’re sure. I wish someone had told me that about geometry.
transcripts.morphology: Matching again: the two roots and the two little front parts. I adore roots. A word that means to look can grow into something grand to stare at, and a word that means to build can end up meaning to tear down, depending on what you put in front. Say a word you know aloud before you match. Then ask which part is doing the work.
transcripts.vocabulary: There’s a little menu of ways to show what you know, and you only pick one. I would want to do all five, but I’m learning that choosing is a skill too. Pick the one you could do best, not the one that sounds grandest. I’ve learned that the hard way. Then use the words as if they were your own. They are, now.
transcripts.grammar: Six sentences, each telling you what kind of verb something is, and some of them are fibbing. Only tap the fibs. For every one, use the test: put was where the verb is and see whether the sentence still makes sense. I used to think every verb was full of action. Most of mine were, I suppose.
transcripts.spelling: Six comparing words, and some are made all wrong, with too many endings piled on, or more stuck in front of a word that already has an ending. I used to pile on extra words exactly like that, to sound grand. Now I try to say a thing once, properly. Tap only the ones that say it twice, or say it wrong.
transcripts.guide2: There’s a box here about knowing who you are. It sounds like something you’d find out all at once, like a fairy in a dell. It isn’t, I’ve discovered. It comes in little bits, and one of them came on Marilla’s lap, in the kitchen, in my new green dress. Read, and watch what I tell her. Then decide whether I was right.
transcripts.wgrd: The box says a big idea has to hold up twice. I like that. It’s like trying on a dress in front of two different mirrors. So when you think you’ve found what this week is really about, take it back to another chapter and see if it still fits. If it doesn’t, it was only one page’s idea. Keep going until it fits both.
transcripts.read: This chapter has a leaving in it, and a lonely little room, and Josie Pye, which is a very odd mixture. There’s one stop, at the end. Before you get there, watch what I hold onto and what I let go. And watch the last page, because something happens there that makes everything feel enormous again. I won’t say what. I’m trying to be less dramatic.
transcripts.guide3: Now the writing. I used to answer every question with three paragraphs and a poem. Miss Stacy taught me that the short way is stronger. So answer what’s asked, in plain words, and prove it with something from the book. If you quote me, quote me exactly. I chose those words very carefully, even the little ones.
transcripts.chapter: The first question wants what I told Marilla, with the picture of the tree in it. The second is about the scholarship, and why I went to bed with my cheeks tingling. The third asks you to look back over the whole week. That one’s the hardest, and the best. Look for what I say out loud, and what you can only see.
transcripts.workshop: The last edit is your ears. Read your whole story out loud, slowly, the way you’d recite at a concert, and wherever you stumble, something is wrong. Fix it. Then say what you’re proud of. That part felt like boasting to me at first. It isn’t. Knowing what you did well is how you do it again.

a.raw: anne was homesick on her first night her room felt strange and small
a.fixed: Anne was homesick on her first night. Her room felt strange and small.
a.why: A capital on Anne, a period after night, a capital H to start the next sentence, and a period at the end. Was and felt are linking verbs.

b.raw: josie pye was no comfort she talked about herself
b.why: Capitals on Josie Pye, a period after comfort, a capital S to start the next sentence, and a period at the end. Was is a linking verb; talked is an action verb.

scholar.journal-q1: … and say whether you think Anne is right that she hasn’t really changed, using one thing from this week.
scholar.journal-q2: … and say what her reaction shows about how her ambitions have grown since Ch. 31.
scholar.journal-q3: … then test your implied theme against a second chapter from this week.

notes.wgrd: A theme has to hold up more than once. Test your big idea on a second scene; if it doesn’t fit, change it until it fits both.
vocab: A strong desire to achieve something important.
Calmness; the ability to stay steady, especially under pressure.
Open to new ideas; willing to consider different points of view.
Careful not to hurt other people’s feelings; thoughtful in dealing with people.
notes.wordParts: spect means “to look” (inspect, respect). struct means “to build” (construct, instruct).
notes.grammar: A linking verb joins the subject to a word that describes or renames it: Anne was happy. Some verbs, like felt and looked, can do either job. The test: can you swap in was?
notes.spelling: One syllable: add -er or -est (small, smallest). Three or more syllables: use more or most (most difficult). Two syllables ending in y: change the y to i, then add the ending (funny, funnier).
